doc.title: Ralph Humphrey interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 11, 2003

title: Great rhythm sections and playing on top of, behind or on the beat
summary: Humphrey cites Chambers, Cobb and Kelly and Richard Davis, and explains controlling where you place the time, pushing versus laying back, and Steve Gadd's time.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Are there other rhythm sections that, if you were given an assignment to drummers or bass players to say go listen to these rhythm sections, who else might you demand they hear?
Well I think you’ve got to mention Paul Chambers and Jimmy Cobb and Wynton Kelly. I think you have to mention Mel Lewis — who was the bass player with—
Richard Davis was on some of that.

Richard Davis. That was an interesting relationship there. When I listen to it it works, but Richard is so on top. And normally the bass player is not on top, it’s the drummer that’s on top. But in this case Richard is just pushing like crazy. But it creates this feel. And it was the same thing with Ron and Tony but Tony was on top. But it creates this thing.
You know it’s like how does that possibly work, if someone’s pushing the beat, how can it not speed up? © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

Well in many cases it does. But what I tell my students is you want to have control over where you’re putting the time. The time is here. Okay now how do you want to relate to that time. You want to be pushing it or do you want to be sort of holding back on it, depending on the style, and then can you control that. And it’s subtle but it creates a feel, and that’s where rhythm sections — they work or they don’t work. Because they somehow created a feel that’s working, and it’s the relationship of where they are to where the beat is.
Yeah. Is it safe to say that if a drummer is pushing a beat maybe not all of his limbs are pushing the beat? Maybe it’s just the ride cymbal or something?
